rationale: A wins because it keeps Peloton's strongest real stories separated and does not need invented consumer theater to sharpen them. Its "Peloton would rather rent you a bike than sell you one" is a defensible model lens; B's "Peloton stopped selling bikes and started renting them" is the same idea with a false verb. B asks some sharp uncomfortable questions, but questions do not disinfect "$2,000" claims and a stop-selling premise the update never gave it.
gaps_in_A: "positive adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow for the first time in three years" smuggles "first time" onto free cash flow; the update only supports the first profitable quarter claim.
"The $200 million diet: how Peloton's new CEO reached an adjusted profit" is a workable operator angle, but it rests on missing CEO identity, tenure, cut details, and interview access.
"from a position it can call strength" gives the rental expansion a little too much company-spin oxygen while the same update says net losses and significant debt remain.
gaps_in_B: "Peloton stopped selling bikes and started renting them" is false on the supplied facts; nationwide rental expansion is not stopping bike sales.
"$2,000+ upfront purchase" and "$2,000 bike" are invented from outside the update and become load-bearing in two angles.
"changes who buys Peloton" and "a customer who was never going to put a four-figure purchase on a card" assert a demographic shift with no rental-member data.
"Peloton posts its first profitable quarter" drops the adjusted/net-loss caveat in the headline after correctly warning that this is exactly how you lose the reporter.
